title: Power
notes: **Definition of power:** Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. P = dW/dt = dE/dt, where W is work, E is energy, and t is time. Average power = W/t; instantaneous power = lim_{Δt→0} ΔW/Δt = dW/dt.

**Formula for power:** Since W = F·s for constant force in the direction of motion, power P = W/t = F·s/t = F·(s/t) = Fv, where v is velocity. This form P = Fv is valid when F and v are in the same direction.

**Units of power:** The SI unit is the watt (W): 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 kg·m²/s³. In engineering, the horsepower (hp) is used: 1 hp (mechanical) = 746 W ≈ 550 ft·lb/s. Kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W is used for engines and appliances.

**Why P = Fv matters:** Power is the product of force and velocity. For a given engine power, you can calculate the max speed when pushing against a force: v = P/F. Example: a motor with 1000 W lifting water has v = 1000/F where F is the weight per second.

**Power for variable force:** For a variable force F(t) acting on an object with velocity v(t), instantaneous power is P(t) = F(t)·v(t). In vector form: P = F·v = |F||v|cos θ (dot product), so power is positive when F and v have the same direction (force aids motion), negative when opposite (force opposes motion).

**Gravitational power:** When lifting an object of mass m at constant speed v, the power required is P = mgh/t = mg(v) = mgv. This is the rate at which gravitational potential energy is increased. For a falling object, P = mgv downward.

**Power in circular motion:** When a particle moves in a circle with speed v, the centripetal force F = mv²/r is perpendicular to velocity. Power = F·v = Fv cos 90° = 0! A centripetal force does no work — it only changes direction, not speed.

**Average power in variable processes:** In processes where power varies (e.g., accelerating car, oscillating pendulum), average power = total work/total time = ΔE/dt. The energy delivered equals the area under the P-t graph.
**Efficiency and power:** No engine is 100% efficient. Input power × efficiency = useful output power. The difference is lost as heat or sound. For a motor with 80% efficiency, P_out = 0.8 × P_input.

**Power in rotational motion:** For rotational systems, power P = τω, where τ is torque and ω is angular velocity (radians/second). Since power = energy/time, and work W = τθ (torque × angular displacement), then P = τθ/t = τω.

**Relationship between power, energy, and time:** E = Pt. If a 100 W device runs for 2 hours, it uses E = 100 × 7200 = 7.2 × 10⁵ J = 200 Wh = 0.2 kWh (kilowatt-hour, the standard energy unit for electricity bills).

**Power rating of devices:** The power rating on appliances (100 W light bulb, 1500 W hair dryer, 2000 W kettle) tells you energy consumption rate, not total energy used. Total energy = power × time of operation. The 60W bulb uses less energy than 100W over the same duration.
confusion: Power and work are NOT the same. Work is energy transfer (measured in Joules); power is the rate of that transfer (measured in Watts). A marathon runner does a lot of work (over 200,000 J) but low power (sustained effort). A sprinter does less total work but very high power.

P = Fv is NOT the same as F·v when the force is not parallel to velocity. The dot product gives P = Fv cos θ, so if F and v are perpendicular (/Centripetal), power is zero. Students often misuse P = Fv without considering the angle.

A more powerful engine does NOT necessarily accelerate faster from rest if it has low torque. Power = τω, so high power at high RPM (low torque) may not move the car quickly from a standstill. Horsepower and torque are related but different — both matter for acceleration.

Energy consumption is power × time, not power alone. A 100 W device and a 50 W device use the same energy if they run for the same duration. The 100 W device delivers energy twice as fast, but total energy depends on how long it runs.

The power rating on a device (e.g., 60 W for an incandescent bulb) is the max power when operated at design voltage. Actual power can vary with line voltage — a bulb at higher voltage runs brighter (more power) but burns out faster.
practice: A pump lifts 50 kg of water to a height of 10 m in 5 seconds. Find the power required. (g = 9.8 m/s²). Solution: Work done = mgh = 50 × 9.8 × 10 = 4900 J. Power = W/t = 4900/5 = 980 W ≈ 1 kW.

A car travels at 30 m/s (108 km/h) against a resisting force of 400 N. Find the engine's power. Solution: P = Fv = 400 × 30 = 12,000 W = 12 kW. At this speed, the engine outputs 12 kW of useful power, assuming no losses.

An engine delivers 50 hp. What is its power in watts? If it runs at 2000 RPM with a wheel radius of 15 cm, find the force exerted at the rim. Solution: 50 hp = 50 × 746 = 37,300 W. Angular velocity ω = 2000 rev/min = 2000 × 2π/60 = 209.4 rad/s. P = τω → τ = P/ω = 37300/209.4 = 178.1 N·m. Force at rim: F = τ/r = 178.1/0.15 = 1187 N.

A person runs up a 10 m staircase in 5 seconds. If the person's mass is 70 kg, what is their average power output? Solution: Height gain = 10 m. Work = mgh = 70 × 9.8 × 10 = 6860 J. Power = 6860 J / 5 s = 1372 W. This is about twice the power of a light bulb!

A 100 W light bulb operates for 10 hours. How much energy is consumed in kilowatt-hours? If electricity costs $0.12 per kWh, what is the cost? Solution: E = Pt = 100 W × 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh. Cost = 1 kWh × $0.12/kWh = $0.12.
universalFacts: The watt (W) is named after James Watt (1736-1819), inventor of the steam engine. He defined 1 horsepower as the power needed to lift 550 pounds one foot in one second, which came out to ~746 W.

Power is a RATE, not a stock. You can have high power for a short time (explosion) or low power for a long time (slow heating), producing the same total energy. This is why endurance athletes often have lower power output than sprinters.
The SI unit of power is the watt: 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 kg·m²/s³. One horsepower (hp) = 746 W exactly (defined value). A 100 W incandescent bulb, if operated 8 hours/day, uses 0.8 kWh/day.
In mechanical systems, power is transmitted through shafts via torque. The power in a rotating shaft is P = τω. The SI unit is watts, and the imperial unit is horsepower (1 hp = 550 ft·lb/s = 746 W).
Einstein's E = mc² represents an enormous power: 1 kg mass converted completely would release 9 × 10¹⁶ J → that's the power equivalent of a billion 100 W bulbs running for one second.
